This vignette shows the three things most analyses need: estimating a single
linear functional, contrasting two of them, and chaining functionals for a
longitudinal regime. Nuisance functions are fit with `glm()` and `lm()` to keep
the examples fast and dependency-free; in practice you would substitute any
learner, ideally cross-fitted (see the *Cross-fitted Super Learning with nadir*
vignette).

```{r setup}
library(RieszCML)
```

## 1. A counterfactual mean

We simulate a point-treatment study with a binary outcome, so the truth
$E[Y^1] = E[P(Y = 1 \mid A = 1, L)]$ can be computed by numerical integration.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
n <- 2000
L <- rnorm(n)
A <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(0.5 * L))
Y <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.5 + A + 0.8 * L))
df <- data.frame(L = L, A = A, Y = Y)

truth_mu1 <- integrate(function(l) plogis(0.5 + 0.8 * l) * dnorm(l), -Inf, Inf)$value
truth_mu0 <- integrate(function(l) plogis(-0.5 + 0.8 * l) * dnorm(l), -Inf, Inf)$value
```

A `RieszCurve` describes the functional: the fitted nuisances (`nuis`), the
Riesz representer at the observed data (`alpha`), the regression whose residual
it multiplies (`f`), the plug-in under the intervention (`h`), and the
uncentered efficient influence function (`ic_expr`). The `alpha_star` and
`targeting_steps` arguments tell the TMLE how to update the counterfactual
predictions.

```{r}
rc_mu1 <- RieszCurve$new(
  nuis = function(data) {
    m_fit <- glm(Y ~ A + L, family = binomial(), data = data)
    g_fit <- glm(A ~ L, family = binomial(), data = data)
    data1 <- data
    data1$A <- 1
    list(
      m  = predict(m_fit, newdata = data,  type = "response"),  # E[Y | A, L]
      m1 = predict(m_fit, newdata = data1, type = "response"),  # E[Y | A = 1, L]
      g  = predict(g_fit, newdata = data,  type = "response")   # P(A = 1 | L)
    )
  },
  alpha = ~ A / g,
  f = ~ m,
  h = ~ m1,
  ic_expr = ~ h + alpha * (Y - f),
  alpha_star = ~ 1 / g,
  targeting_steps = list(m = list(), m1 = list(alpha_star = ~ 1 / g))
)
```

The one-step estimator averages the influence function; the TMLE instead
updates the fitted regressions, which keeps the estimate within the bounds of
the outcome.

```{r}
fit_os <- riesz_estimate(df, rc_mu1)
fit_os

fit_tmle <- riesz_tmle(df, rc_mu1, fluctuation_type = "logistic",
                       bounds = c(0, 1), outcome_col = "Y")
fit_tmle

c(one_step = fit_os$estimate, tmle = fit_tmle$estimate, truth = truth_mu1)
```

## 2. Contrasts: the average treatment effect and risk ratio

Common functionals are available in `riesz_curve_catalog`, which builds the
same kind of curve from a `nuis` function alone. Here we fit $E[Y^0]$ and
combine it with the fit above using the delta method. All fits must use the
same data, so their influence functions line up row by row.

```{r}
rc_mu0 <- riesz_curve_catalog$cfmean_a(
  a = 0,
  nuis = function(data) {
    m_fit <- glm(Y ~ A + L, family = binomial(), data = data)
    g_fit <- glm(I(A == 0) ~ L, family = binomial(), data = data)
    data0 <- data
    data0$A <- 0
    list(
      m  = predict(m_fit, newdata = data,  type = "response"),
      ma = predict(m_fit, newdata = data0, type = "response"),
      g  = predict(g_fit, newdata = data,  type = "response")   # P(A = 0 | L)
    )
  }
)

fit_mu0 <- riesz_tmle(df, rc_mu0, fluctuation_type = "logistic",
                      bounds = c(0, 1), outcome_col = "Y")

fit_ate <- riesz_delta_difference(fit_tmle, fit_mu0, parameter = "ATE")
fit_rr  <- riesz_delta_ratio(fit_tmle, fit_mu0, parameter = "Risk ratio")

fit_ate
c(ate = fit_ate$estimate, truth = truth_mu1 - truth_mu0)
c(rr = fit_rr$estimate, truth = truth_mu1 / truth_mu0)
```

## 3. A nested functional: a two-time-point regime

The mean outcome under treatment at both time points, $E[Y^{1,1}]$, is a
sequence of two regressions. Each stage is its own `RieszCurve`, and
`ComposedRieszCurve` chains them. Stages are supplied **innermost first**: the
first stage regresses `Y`, and the second regresses the first stage's plug-in,
which it sees as a column named `` `h[j=1]` ``.

```{r}
set.seed(2)
n <- 5000
L1 <- rnorm(n)
A1 <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.2 + L1))
L2 <- 0.5 + 0.7 * L1 + 2 * A1 + rnorm(n)
A2 <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.3 + 0.6 * A1 + 1.2 * L2))
Y  <- 1 + 1.5 * L2 + 3 * A2 + rnorm(n)
df_long <- data.frame(L1, A1, L2, A2, Y)

truth_mu11 <- 1 + 1.5 * (0.5 + 2) + 3   # = 7.75

rc_t2 <- RieszCurve$new(            # innermost stage: time 2
  nuis = function(data) {
    m_fit <- lm(Y ~ L1 + A1 + L2 + A2, data = data)
    g_fit <- glm(A2 ~ L1 + A1 + L2, family = binomial(), data = data)
    d1 <- data
    d1$A2 <- 1
    list(m  = predict(m_fit, newdata = data),
         m1 = predict(m_fit, newdata = d1),
         g  = predict(g_fit, newdata = data, type = "response"))
  },
  alpha = ~ A2 / g, alpha_star = ~ 1 / g,
  f = ~ m, h = ~ m1,
  ic_expr = ~ h + alpha * (Y - f)
)

rc_t1 <- RieszCurve$new(            # outermost stage: time 1
  nuis = function(data) {
    m_fit <- lm(`h[j=1]` ~ L1 + A1, data = data)
    g_fit <- glm(A1 ~ L1, family = binomial(), data = data)
    d1 <- data
    d1$A1 <- 1
    list(m  = predict(m_fit, newdata = data),
         m1 = predict(m_fit, newdata = d1),
         g  = predict(g_fit, newdata = data, type = "response"))
  },
  alpha = ~ A1 / g, alpha_star = ~ 1 / g,
  f = ~ m, h = ~ m1,
  ic_expr = ~ h + alpha * (`h[j=1]` - f)
)

rc_11 <- ComposedRieszCurve$new(rc_list = list(rc_t2, rc_t1))

fit_11_os   <- riesz_estimate(df_long, rc_11)
fit_11_tmle <- riesz_tmle(df_long, rc_11, fluctuation_type = "logistic",
                          bounds = range(df_long$Y) + c(-1, 1),
                          outcome_col = "Y")

c(one_step = fit_11_os$estimate, tmle = fit_11_tmle$estimate, truth = truth_mu11)
```

Every stage of a composed TMLE needs `alpha_star`, the representer evaluated
under that stage's intervention. For a continuous outcome, the logistic
fluctuation needs `bounds` that contain every observed outcome; padding the
observed range, as above, is a simple choice.
